english.html: no less that, under this mantle of rigour and severity of penalty, they wholly efface, or at least in part purge, and clean a little, the filth of their evil life, their corruptions and detestable vices: without thinking that we are all Christians, and children of one heavenly Father, regenerated by one Baptism, and by it incorporated into the Church of God, redeemed by the one blood of Jesus Christ, our head, of whom we are all members, and under whose banner we battle against Satan, the common enemy of nature, who surrounds us day and night to devour us; wherefore, if he catches one of us, all ought to try to bear his burden and his load, by pity, gentleness, compassion and mercy <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. And we ought moreover to consider that with judgments it is as with victories, of which that which is won without the shedding of human blood is always the noblest and the most acceptable before God. Not that I would thereby take away the sword, which I well know to be given to magistrates for the vengeance of malefactors, and to do justice in wrath (says the Apostle) upon him that does evil <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. For I am not ignorant that, as Publilius the Mime-writer has left written: Whosoever spares the wicked, harms the good.

notes.gloss: "Bear ye one another's burdens"; restore the fallen brother in the spirit of meekness.

notes.citation: First Epistle of Peter, chapter 2 (1 Peter 2:14)
notes.original: La premiere S. Pierre c. ij.
notes.gloss: Governors are sent "for the punishment of evildoers"; Coras's words en ire … de celuy qui fait mal are those of Romans 13:4, "a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil", which he runs together with the Peter text.

english.html: Bonis nocet, quisquis pepercerit malis [He harms the good who spares the wicked].

And that the sharpness and severity of penalties is sometimes the teaching and discipline of living well. <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup> But I mean that this must be done with great circumspection and prudence, and that judges must not readily make themselves prodigal of the blood of their Christian brother, but rather exercise themselves more in humanity and clemency than in rigour and cruelty — and the sovereign judges especially: both because there is nothing so ugly, so base, nor so deformed as to add to a sovereign power a sharpness and acerbity of nature <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>, and because also they ought to serve as examples to their inferiors and, like lamps, give light to all the others. Wherefore, when it shall be fitting to put the malefactor to death for his demerits, let it be without the horror and confusion of these cruel and barbarous spectacles, unless it be for some great, horrible and enor

notes.original: Aule Gelle au xx. liu. c⟨alt:c.⟩ j.
notes.gloss: The debate of Favorinus and Sextus Caecilius on the Twelve Tables, where Caecilius defends their severity: the harshness of punishing wrongdoing is a discipline of living well and carefully (acerbitas plerumque ulciscendi maleficii bene atque caute vivendi disciplina est, 20.1.53).

notes.citation: Cicero, Letters to his brother Quintus, book 1, letter 1 (Ad Q. fratrem 1.1.37)
notes.original: Ciceron en l'epiſtre i. ad Q⟨alt:Q.⟩ fratrem.
notes.gloss: Nihil est tam deforme quam ad summum imperium etiam acerbitatem naturae adiungere: nothing is so unseemly as to add to supreme power a natural harshness.
